value: non-luminescent fish (non-functional light organs) showed no change in blink frequency after shrimp larvae hatched and captured only approximately 10% of the shrimp captured when compared with luminescent fish
units: % of shrimp larvae captured relative to luminescent fish
method: aquarium behaviour: luminescent and non-luminescent splitfin flashlight fish given hatching cleaner-shrimp larvae at night, blink frequency and larvae capture recorded under 850 nm infrared illumination
conditions: captive: specimens bought from a commercial wholesaler (De Jong Marinelife, Netherlands) and captured at Cebu Island, Philippines, kept on a 12 h light/dark cycle; 5 luminescent and 3 non-luminescent fish used in the behaviour experiments (from an initial 9 luminescent and 14 non-luminescent); the non-luminescent fish were not experimentally blocked: their light organs had degenerated (fewer tubules, lost blood vessels), which the authors attribute most likely to food deprivation during transport, so fish condition is confounded with light emission; apparently the same fish across repeated sessions (two 5-minute sessions); sex not reported; trials 2 h after lights-off, no light intensity given for them; number of larvae and capture scoring method not reported, and no test statistic for the capture comparison (the repeated-measures ANOVA results are given for blink frequency only); luminous fish cut blink frequency to 18.6 +/- 4.7% of the unfed night level after hatching began (ANOVA F = 58.074, P < 0.001); the page summary says non-luminous fish could not find food under the infrared lighting; the abstract also gives about 90 blinks/min at night and about 9 blinks/min by day in a cave

value: locomotor activity almost completely inhibited when moonlight was shadowed during three lunar eclipses
method: long-term actimetry on free-ranging owl monkeys: Actiwatch AW4 collar activity in 5-minute bins compared with moonlight, including three lunar eclipses
conditions: wild Azara's owl monkeys captured in gallery forest along the Guaycolec River and collared, n = 10 individuals recorded for 6 to 18 months, recaptured at 3 to 6 months to retrieve or refit collars; sex of all ten not stated (two males shown in a figure); luminance came from a remote photocell on a 2-m post pointed at the zenith in an open savannah area next to the study site, so the monkeys' own light levels were probably 1 to 2 log units lower, and luminance data existed for nine animals; contrary and context figures from the page summary: 36.6 +/- 0.9% of total daily activity still fell in fully dark night hours, nocturnal activity (21:00 to 06:00) was 51.6 +/- 1.1% of daily total on full-moon nights against 25.9 +/- 1.0% on new-moon nights, and temperature also masked activity; the eclipse comparison is a Friedman test (X2 = 32.35, df = 8, p printed as 0.000), full eclipse lower than partial eclipse, penumbra and the periods before and after; subjects per eclipse are given only in the Figure 3 panels

measured_endpoint: number of consecutive nights a female glowed (taken as time to mating)
intervention: existing low-pressure sodium streetlighting (0.017 to 8.53 lux at the female)
mechanism_limit: glow duration is an inferred mating outcome, not a measure of what males or females see; site, light and female origin are not separated
value: females in dark surroundings typically stopped glowing after one night, whereas females in illuminated areas glowed for significantly more nights, in some cases up to 15
method: field monitoring of female glowing status (a proxy for mating status) in dark versus streetlit sites over the mating season
conditions: Lippelo, Belgium (Lippelobos and Speelbos Marselaere); 51 females, 24 in dark areas (0.008 to 0.020 lux) and 27 in lit areas (0.017 to 8.53 lux, monochromatic orange low-pressure sodium lighting), median 6 consecutive nights glowing in lit areas (range 1 to 15); mixed origin: some females found in situ, others raised in captivity from field-collected larvae, 28 found in situ (19 monitored where found, 9 relocated: 8 lit to dark, 1 between lit conditions) and 23 reared; all 24 dark-area females (4 in situ, 12 reared, 8 translocated) stopped glowing after one night; observational and not randomised, so site, light and female origin are not separated; glow cessation is an inferred, not observed, mating; the survival analysis found time to mating increased with ambient light intensity (estimate -0.598, S.E. 0.125, p printed as '> 0.001', probably a typo for < 0.001); females were 'arbitrarily' chosen and released, not randomised

measured_endpoint: presence and feeding of hedgehogs recorded by camera trap at the feeding station, per ten-minute block
experimental_unit: ten-minute block at a garden feeding station (33 gardens; individuals not identified)
intervention: one week of constant artificial light on the feeding station at night (the station's existing exterior light or, where none was suitable, a supplied LED floodlight of about 1,000 lumens, 10 W)
comparator: one week of darkness at the same station
mechanism_limit: camera-event counts combine activity, local availability and detectability; no sensory pathway is tested, and a null does not show that light is not perceived
value: no overall impact of artificial light at night on the presence or feeding activity of hedgehogs at supplementary feeding stations (null result)
method: citizen-science camera-trap crossover: one week of artificial light and one week of darkness at each garden feeding station
conditions: wild hedgehogs visiting 33 gardens in England and Wales, 15 July to 21 August 2017, the station's existing exterior light or, where none was suitable, a supplied LED floodlight of about 1,000 lumens (10 W), so intensity was not matched across stations; treatment order was not randomised (dark first at dark stations, light first at already lit stations), so order is tied to the station's lighting history; 3,470 of 22,615 ten-minute blocks held hedgehogs (1,724 dark, 1,746 light); odds ratio for presence 1.00 (95% CI 0.92 to 1.09), for feeding 0.99 (0.91 to 1.10); contrary to the null, activity patterns differed between treatments at 13 of 31 sites but the direction was inconsistent; individuals not recognised, and age and sex not recorded; stations already habituated to feeding

value: when the chamber was illuminated 9 of 10 rats still crossed into the opposing chamber, but rate of movement fell by 40%
method: outdoor U-maze test from dusk to morning, one rat per night, lit chamber against dark chamber, between-subject
conditions: wild-caught from native forest in Canterbury, New Zealand, housed at Lincoln University; 20 rats (10 male, 10 female) tested once each in August 2016, one excluded so 19 analysed; about 1,000 lux illuminated versus under 1 lux dark; food deprived 12 h; light assigned between animals in blocks (5 males and 5 females each); null results: no change in foraging measures (latency to seed tray, visits, time per visit, total foraging duration, foraging rate); the same paper gives 53% fewer visits and a drop in crossings by 70% (the Abstract words the 70% as less exploration), and males spent 45 fewer minutes in the lit chamber (p = 0.05) while females did not change (p = 0.34); only three of seven movement behaviours changed significantly (Abstract) and the other four did not, including a visit duration trend about twice as long (p = 0.07); test statistics are in a table not read

value: circadian rhythm of locomotor activity abolished under 12:12 light-dark (p = 0.60) and constant light (p = 0.242)
method: locomotor activity of groups of workers recorded under constant darkness (DD), 12:12 light-dark (LD) and constant light (LL) at 100 lux, tested for circadian rhythmicity
conditions: workers from field colonies collected at Shizi Hill, Wuhan, China and brought to the laboratory (seven colonies for this species, as read from the summary); six workers per 9 cm dish, so the unit is probably the dish (the Figure 3 legend does not say whether n counts dishes or workers, or whether colonies were pooled), n about 10 (DD), 9 (LD) and 9 (LL); LD 08:00 to 20:00 Beijing time; the same paper finds a significant free-running rhythm in DD (p < 0.001, period close to 24 h), so 'abolished' means loss of statistical rhythmicity under light, not loss of activity; under LL daytime activity was lower than at night (Z = -3.58, p < 0.001), under LD no day-night difference (Z = -1.28, p = 0.20) and under DD daytime activity was higher; Reticulitermes chinensis, also named in the sentence, gave the same result but is not filed here
